newsitem.title: USA: Retailers file antitrust suit against Visa.
newsitem.headline: Retailers file antitrust suit against Visa.

text.p: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. and the Limited Inc. have filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Visa USA alleging that retailers are being forced to accept a type of debit card for which they must pay "exorbitant" fees.

The suit, filed in Brooklyn federal court last week, seeks unspecified damages. It alleges that the retailers are paying hundreds of millions of dollars in fees, and if the antitrust allegations are proven, the damage amount, to be decided by the court, could be trebled.

The suit alleges that all retailers who accept the Visa credit card are being forced to accept Visa Check, which is a type of debit card that allows money from the customer's bank account to be transferred to the retailer.
Visa Check is described in the suit as being an "off-line" debit card that electronically transfers money in one to five days after the sales transaction.

Off-line cards differ from "on-line" debit cards that allow the immediate transfer of money from customers' accounts. The retailers alleged that the off-line cards are less secure, allowing for greater fraud and greater losses for both consumers and retailers.
The suit alleges that the retailers have contacted Visa and demanded that they be allowed to accept Visa credit cards without taking Visa Check. Visa allegedly refused.
Visa issued a statement vowing to defend itself, saying it "believes there is absolutely no merit in this case." A Visa spokesman could not immediately be reached for comment Friday.

"Wal-Mart, The Limited and class members did not and do not want to accept Visa Check because the fees charged for Visa Check are exorbitant, fixed and maintained at supra-competitive levels only through the coercive force of the tying arrangement," the suit states.
The retailers allege that they are prohibited by Visa from asking customers if they would pay for their purchases by other debit cards such as NYCE or MAC, which charge retailers lower fees.

The suit alleges that when Wal-Mart and the Limited accept Visa Check for a $100 purchase, the interchange fee is at least $1.10. In comparison, the fees for NYCE and MAC debit cards are about 75 cents and 65 cents respectively.

It alleges that in 1995 Visa Check cards were used in about 556 million retail transactions, comprising a dollar volume of about $22 billion. The interchange fees computed at the lowest possible rate for these transactions was about $250 million, the suit alleges.
It alleges that retailers would have paid less than $33 million in interchange fees for the same transactions processed by on-line debit networks.

The plaintiffs also allege that Visa has tried to deceive retailers into believing they were receiving the Visa credit card instead of Visa Check. The suit alleges that some retailers do not even know they are accepting Visa Check because the debit card is electronically and visually indistinguishable from a Visa credit card.
"Over the years, Visa carefully, relentlessly and stealthily fostered the domination of Visa Check over faster, safer and far less costly on-line point of sale debit networks," the suit alleges.
It alleges that since 1992, the number of Visa Check cards has increased by an average of 56 percent and the average rate of increase in Visa Check transactions during this period was 60 percent.
Last year alone, the number of transactions increased by 80 percent, the suit alleges.
